title: World History: The Big Picture · Episode 3
chapters: World War I and the ANZACs
World War II: how it began and ended

units.t: World History: The Big Picture. Episode three.
In this episode: World War I and the ANZACs, World War II: how it began and ended and The Cold War.
Part one. World War I and the ANZACs.
The war that was meant to be over by Christmas lasted four years, killed millions and shaped Australia's sense of itself.
A spark, then a chain.
On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot dead in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist.
Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war a month later.
Why did a regional crisis spread?
Europe was split into alliance blocs: Germany and Austria-Hungary on one side, France, Russia and Britain on the other.
Countries had huge armies and war plans that relied on mobilising quickly.
Empires competed for colonies and naval power, and nationalism ran high.
Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria-Hungary, and when Germany invaded neutral Belgium to attack France, Britain declared war.
As part of the British Empire, Australia was automatically at war.
Trenches and new weapons.
Everyone expected a short war.
Instead, by late 1914 the Western Front was a line of trenches from the Belgian coast to Switzerland.
Machine guns, barbed wire and artillery made attacking across 'no man's land' suicidal, and huge offensives gained only a few kilometres at enormous cost.
On the first day of the Somme in 1916, the British Army suffered about 57,000 casualties.
Soldiers lived with mud, rats, lice, disease and constant shelling.
It was an industrial war with terrible new weapons.
Poison gas, first used on a large scale in 1915, caused blindness and suffocation.
Tanks appeared in 1916.
Aircraft moved from scouting to bombing.
German submarine attacks on shipping helped bring the United States into the war in 1917.
Gallipoli and sacrifice.
In 1915 the Allies tried to knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war by seizing the Dardanelles strait.
On 25 April, the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landed at what became known as Anzac Cove.
They faced steep cliffs and determined Ottoman defenders.
The campaign dragged on for eight months before the Allies withdrew.
About 8,700 Australians died.
The day of the landing became Anzac Day.
Australia had fewer than five million people, yet about 417,000 men enlisted, all volunteers; two referendums on conscription were narrowly defeated.
More than 60,000 died and around 156,000 were wounded, gassed or taken prisoner.
Most deaths came on the Western Front, at places like Pozieres, Fromelles and Passchendaele.
More than 1,000 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander men also served, despite discrimination at home.
The end.
In 1917 Russia collapsed into revolution and left the war, but American troops and resources tipped the balance towards the Allies.
Germany's final offensives in 1918 failed, its allies surrendered and its people were starving.
An armistice took effect at 11 am on 11 November 1918, the 'eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month', now marked as Remembrance Day.
Around 20 million soldiers and civilians had died.
The influenza pandemic that followed killed tens of millions more.
Medicine had advanced too, with blood transfusions, better surgery and new understanding of what was then called 'shell shock'.
A flawed peace.
The 1919 Treaty of Versailles forced Germany to accept blame, give up territory and colonies, limit its army and pay heavy reparations.
Australian Prime Minister Billy Hughes was there and fought for Australia to control German New Guinea.
Four empires, the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman, had collapsed, redrawing maps across Europe and the Middle East.
Many Germans resented the treaty bitterly.
That resentment helped fuel the rise of Hitler and a second, even deadlier world war just 20 years later.
A peace that humiliates the loser can plant the seeds of the next conflict.
The key idea: A single assassination in 1914 became a world war because of rival alliances, huge armies and imperial rivalry.
Part two. World War II: how it began and ended.
The deadliest conflict in human history, and how it still shapes the world you live in.
The road to war.
World War II ran from 1939 to 1945 and was the deadliest conflict in human history, with an estimated 70 to 85 million deaths, most of them civilians.
It drew in most nations, including every great power, and was fought across Europe, Africa, Asia and the Pacific.
Around a million Australians served, from a population of about seven million, and nearly 40,000 died.
It grew from the aftermath of World War I.
Germany faced harsh terms under the Treaty of Versailles, including lost territory and reparations.
Then the Great Depression brought mass unemployment.
Adolf Hitler and the Nazis exploited the anger, took power in 1933, built a dictatorship and rearmed.
Britain and France tried appeasement, giving in to some demands, such as letting Germany take part of Czechoslovakia in 1938, to keep the peace.
From Poland to the world.
In August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed a pact not to attack each other, secretly agreeing to divide Poland.
Germany invaded on 1 September.
Britain and France declared war two days later, and Prime Minister Robert Menzies announced that Australia was at war too.
Fast tanks and aircraft swept through western Europe, and France fell in June 1940.
Britain held out in the Battle of Britain.
In June 1941 Hitler broke the pact and invaded the Soviet Union, opening the war's largest and bloodiest front.
In December, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, bringing in the US, and swept through South-East Asia.
Singapore fell in February 1942, with around 15,000 Australians taken prisoner, and Darwin was bombed days later.
The main Allies were Britain and its Commonwealth, the Soviet Union and the US; the Axis was Germany, Italy and Japan.
The Holocaust.
The Nazi regime systematically murdered around six million Jews, about two thirds of Europe's Jewish population, in what is known as the Holocaust or Shoah.
Millions of others were also killed, including Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, Poles and political opponents.
Victims were shot in mass executions or murdered in death camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau.
The scale and deliberate planning shocked the world.
The Holocaust led directly to new international laws on genocide and human rights after the war.
The tide turns.
In 1942 and 1943 the tide turned.
The US defeated Japan's navy at the Battle of Midway in June 1942.
Australian troops halted the Japanese advance on the Kokoda Track in Papua.
British and Commonwealth forces, including Australians, won at El Alamein in Egypt.
The Soviet victory at Stalingrad in early 1943 destroyed an entire German army.
On 6 June 1944, D-Day, Allied troops landed in Normandy, France, opening a second front in the west.
Germany was now squeezed between Soviet forces in the east and the Western Allies.
The end and the legacy.
Hitler took his own life in Berlin, and Germany surrendered in May 1945.
In August the US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing well over 100,000 people, and the Soviet Union declared war on Japan.
Japan announced its surrender on 15 August, now Victory in the Pacific Day in Australia, and signed formally on 2 September.
The war reshaped the world.
The United Nations was founded in 1945 to prevent another global conflict.
The US and Soviet Union became rival superpowers, beginning the Cold War.
European empires weakened and many colonies soon gained independence.
In Australia, the main alliance shifted from Britain towards the US, and a huge postwar migration program, under the slogan 'populate or perish', brought millions from Europe and later the world.
The key idea: World War II, 1939 to 1945, was the deadliest conflict in history, rooted in the aftermath of World War I and the Depression.
Part three. The Cold War.
For over 40 years, two superpowers came close to destroying the world without ever fighting each other directly.
Allies become rivals.
The United States and the Soviet Union fought on the same side in World War II, but had little else in common.
The US was a capitalist democracy; the USSR was a communist one-party state.
As the war ended, Soviet forces controlled Eastern Europe and installed communist governments.
In 1946 Winston Churchill warned that an 'iron curtain' had descended across Europe.
Germany was split into a democratic West and a communist East, and Berlin was split too.
In 1948-49 the Soviets blockaded West Berlin, and the Western allies supplied the city entirely by air for almost a year.
NATO formed in 1949 and the Soviet bloc answered with the Warsaw Pact in 1955.
East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop people fleeing west.
It stood until 1989.
The nuclear arms race.
The US used atomic bombs in 1945, and the Soviet Union tested its own in 1949.
Both sides then raced to build more and bigger weapons, including hydrogen bombs hundreds or even thousands of times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb.
At the peak, in the mid-1980s, there were around 70,000 nuclear warheads in the world.
The strategy was mutually assured destruction, aptly abbreviated MAD.
It held that neither side would attack, because it would be destroyed in return.
The Cold War, roughly 1947 to 1991, was called 'cold' because the superpowers never fought each other directly.
Schoolchildren practised 'duck and cover' drills.
Thirteen days in 1962.
In October 1962, US spy planes discovered Soviet nuclear missiles being installed in Cuba, just 145 kilometres from Florida.
For thirteen tense days, the world stood on the edge of nuclear war.
President John F.
Kennedy ordered a naval blockade of Cuba.
Eventually Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for a US promise not to invade Cuba, and a secret deal to remove US missiles from Turkey.
Afterwards, a direct hotline was set up between Washington and Moscow, so leaders could talk quickly in a crisis.
Rivalry by other means.
Instead of fighting each other, the superpowers backed opposing sides in conflicts around the world.
The Korean War, 1950-53, ended in a stalemate that still divides the peninsula.
In Vietnam, the US fought to stop the communist North taking over the South.
About 60,000 Australians served there between 1962 and 1973, and 523 died.
The war sparked huge protests in Australia, including over conscription.
Proxy conflicts also raged in Afghanistan, Angola and Latin America.
The rivalry extended into space.
The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite, in 1957, and Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space in 1961.
On 20 July 1969 Apollo 11 landed on the Moon.
Honeysuckle Creek and the Parkes radio telescope helped broadcast those first pictures.
The end and the legacy.
By the 1980s the Soviet economy was struggling.
Mikhail Gorbachev, leader from 1985, introduced reforms known as glasnost, openness, and perestroika, restructuring, and signed arms reduction treaties with Ronald Reagan.
In 1989 peaceful revolutions swept Eastern Europe, and on 9 November the Berlin Wall opened.
Germany reunified in 1990, and on 26 December 1991 the Soviet Union dissolved into 15 countries.
The legacy is all around us.
NATO still exists and has expanded.
Thousands of nuclear weapons remain, though far fewer than at the peak.
Satellites, GPS and the early internet came from the rivalry.
Many of today's tensions, from Ukraine to Korea, have roots in Cold War divisions.
The key idea: After World War II the US and Soviet Union became opposing superpowers, and Europe divided into two armed blocs.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did the assassination in Sarajevo grow into a world war?
Answer. Interlocking alliances and war plans pulled in the great powers.
Question two. What was 'appeasement'?
Answer. Giving in to some of Hitler's demands for peace.
Question three. Why was the Cold War called 'cold'?
Answer. The two sides never fought directly.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
